electrical: Japan uses Type A plugs (same as US/Canada - 2 flat prongs). Voltage is 100V (slightly lower than US 120V but all modern chargers, laptops, and phone chargers work perfectly with no adapter). No adapter needed for US travelers. European/UK travelers need a Type A adapter. Some older buildings only have 2-prong outlets (no grounding).

transportation.suica: Get a Suica or Pasmo IC card for seamless travel. For iPhone users, the new Welcome Suica Mobile app (launched March 2025) lets you create a virtual Suica card and top up via Apple Pay - no more hunting for physical cards. It stays valid for 180 days (vs 28 days for physical Welcome Suica). Physical cards available at JR station ticket machines (¥500 deposit). Works on all trains, buses, and at convenience stores/vending machines. By autumn 2025, the app added ticketless Shinkansen travel, and by spring 2026, Green Car support on local lines.
transportation.trainTips: Tokyo's train system is world-class but complex. Key lines: JR Yamanote (the loop line connecting major stations), Tokyo Metro (9 lines), Toei Subway (4 lines). Google Maps is extremely accurate for routing and real-time delays. Trains run approximately 5am-midnight. Rush hour (7:30-9:30am) is intense - avoid with luggage. Train station signage is in English. Platform screens show upcoming trains and destinations.
transportation.lastTrains: Last trains typically run around midnight-12:30am. Miss it and your options are: taxi (~¥3,000-8,000 depending on distance), late-night bus services, manga cafe or internet cafe (¥1,500-3,000 for overnight with free drinks), or capsule hotel. First trains resume around 5:00am. Google Maps will warn you when the last train is approaching.
transportation.apps: Google Maps (best for train routing, extremely accurate), Welcome Suica Mobile (iPhone IC card), Navitime for Japan Travel (backup transit app with English), Japan Transit Planner

apps.name: Google Maps
apps.description: Essential for train routing - extremely accurate in Tokyo with real-time delay info. Shows walking routes, train transfers, platform numbers, and costs.

apps.name: Welcome Suica Mobile
apps.description: Official JR East app (launched March 2025) for iPhone. Create a virtual Suica IC card for contactless transit payments and store purchases. Top up via Apple Pay. Valid 180 days.

apps.name: Tabelog
apps.description: Japan's #1 restaurant review site with millions of reviews. Scores above 3.5 are excellent (top ~5% of restaurants). Scores above 4.0 are exceptional. Has English interface. More trusted locally than Google Reviews.

apps.name: Navitime for Japan Travel
apps.description: Backup transit app with full English support. Good for multi-day trip planning and finding nearby stations.

apps.name: Google Translate
apps.description: Camera mode for real-time translation of menus, signs, and labels. Download Japanese language pack offline before your trip. Conversation mode works well for basic communication.

apps.name: Japan WiFi Auto-Connect
apps.description: Auto-connects to free WiFi hotspots at convenience stores, stations, and public spaces across Japan. Useful backup if your eSIM has data limits.

apps.name: Suica (Apple Wallet)
apps.description: Alternative to Welcome Suica - add a Suica card directly to Apple Wallet. Works for transit, vending machines, and konbini payments. Requires iPhone 8 or later.

apps.name: PayPay
apps.description: Japan's most popular QR payment app (70M+ users), accepted at 3.7M+ locations. Note: requires Japanese phone number to register. However, foreign e-wallet users (Alipay, WeChat Pay, GCash, etc.) can pay at PayPay merchants through partner integrations.

apps.name: XE Currency
apps.description: Real-time currency conversion. Helpful for quickly checking prices when shopping. Download offline rates before your trip.

connectivity.wifi: Free WiFi is spotty outside hotels. Most konbini (7-Eleven, Lawson, FamilyMart) offer free WiFi. Starbucks and major train stations have free WiFi. Consider the Japan WiFi Auto-Connect app to automatically connect to free hotspots across the country.
connectivity.esim: Strongly recommended: Get an eSIM before you travel. Top options for 2025-2026: Airalo (SoftBank network, 5GB/30 days ~$8.50 with sign-up discount, good urban coverage), Ubigi (NTT DOCOMO network, 10GB/30 days ~$17, better rural coverage), or Sim Local (best value for money per GB). Data-only plans start from ~$4-5/week. Much easier than renting a pocket WiFi device. Activate before landing in Japan. Both Airalo and Ubigi have well-rated apps for setup.

luggage: Coin lockers are everywhere in train stations. Small (¥400), Medium (¥500), Large (¥700). Most now accept IC cards (Suica/Pasmo) in addition to coins. For oversized bags, use Yamato Transport (Kuroneko - look for the black cat logo) to ship luggage between hotels for ~¥2,000-3,000 per bag, same-day or next-day delivery. Hotels can arrange this for you. Also available at convenience stores.
etiquette: Never tip - it's considered rude or confusing
Remove shoes when entering homes, some restaurants, and temples (look for shoe racks or a raised entrance area)
Stand on the left side of escalators in Tokyo (right side for walking) - reversed from Osaka
Don't eat while walking - stop to eat street food, find a bench, or eat at the stall
Bow slightly when greeting people - a small nod is fine for tourists
Don't talk on your phone on trains - set to silent mode (manner mode). Texting is fine
Don't blow your nose in public - go to the restroom or step aside discreetly
Sort your trash - Japan has specific bins for burnable, plastic bottles, cans, and glass. Trash cans are rare on streets; carry a small bag
Queue politely - line jumping is seriously frowned upon. Japanese queuing is immaculate
Use two hands when giving/receiving business cards, gifts, or money

Onsen etiquette: Wash thoroughly before entering the bath. No swimsuits. Small towels kept out of the water. Tattoos are increasingly accepted but check the specific onsen first - some have relaxed policies, others still prohibit
It's OK to slurp noodles loudly - it's considered a sign of enjoyment and cools the noodles
Say 'itadakimasu' (I humbly receive) before eating and 'gochisousama deshita' (thank you for the meal) after
Don't point at people - use an open hand gesture instead
Umbrellas: always use the umbrella stand/lock outside shops. Taking the wrong umbrella is a faux pas

weather: Late February in Tokyo: Cold but mild compared to many Western cities. Temperatures around 2-10°C (35-50°F). Occasional rain, rare snow. Low humidity. Pack layers, a warm jacket, and a compact umbrella. Not as cold as many expect. Some early plum blossoms (ume) may be blooming at shrines and parks - a beautiful preview of cherry blossom season coming in late March. Sunset around 5:30pm.

money.cashVsCard: Japan is increasingly card-friendly but still significantly cash-dependent, especially at small restaurants, ramen shops, izakayas, shrines, markets, and many smaller businesses. Always carry ¥10,000-20,000 in cash. 7-Eleven ATMs (Seven Bank) and Japan Post ATMs reliably accept foreign Visa/Mastercard. Convenience store ATMs are available 24/7 in most locations. Visa/Mastercard tap-to-pay acceptance is growing rapidly in 2025-2026.
money.tipping: Never tip in Japan. It can be considered rude or confusing. Service charges are included where applicable. Exceptional service is simply the cultural standard.
money.taxFree: Spend ¥5,000+ (before tax) at a single participating store in one day to get the 10% consumption tax exempted. Look for 'Tax-Free' or '免税' signs. Bring your passport. Major changes coming November 2026: new refund system at airports instead of in-store exemption, potentially allowing combined spending across multiple shops. Current system: show passport at tax-free counter, items are sealed in a bag (consumables) or recorded electronically.

options.steps: Narita Express to Tokyo Station (~60 min, ¥3,250). Transfer to Marunouchi Line toward Ogikubo. Ride 3 stops to Akasaka-mitsuke (~7 min). Walk 5 min to hotel.
Skyliner to Ueno (~41 min, ¥2,520). Transfer to Ginza Line toward Shibuya. Ride to Akasaka-mitsuke (~15 min, ¥200). Walk 5 min to hotel.
Limousine Bus to Akasaka Excel Hotel Tokyu or ANA InterContinental (~100 min). Short walk/taxi to hotel. Comfortable but slower, can get stuck in traffic.
Keikyu Airport Line to Shinagawa (~15 min). Transfer to JR Yamanote or Ginza Line. Easiest: Yamanote to Shimbashi, then Ginza Line to Akasaka-mitsuke. Walk 5 min to hotel.
Monorail to Hamamatsucho (~18 min). Walk to Daimon Station. Toei Oedo Line to Roppongi or Aoyama-itchome, then short transfer or walk.
Direct to hotel. Most convenient, especially late at night or with heavy luggage. Fixed-rate highway taxis available.

akasaka.title: Akasaka — Your Home Base
akasaka.description: A central, well-connected neighborhood mixing business hotels, government buildings, and excellent dining. Quieter than Shinjuku/Shibuya but perfectly positioned to reach everywhere fast.
akasaka.stations: Akasaka-mitsuke (Ginza + Marunouchi Lines), Akasaka (Chiyoda Line), Tameike-Sanno (Ginza + Namboku Lines)
walkable: Hie Shrine (日枝神社) — 5 min walk, beautiful hilltop shrine with unique tunnel of torii gates
TBS Akasaka Sacas — 3 min, entertainment complex with restaurants
Akasaka Biz Tower — 5 min, dining and shopping
Roppongi — 15 min walk (or 1 stop on Chiyoda Line)
Toraya Akasaka — 5 min, legendary wagashi (traditional sweets) shop
akasaka.nearbyFood: The Akasaka area has tons of lunch spots for salarymen. Walk toward Roppongi for nightlife dining, or toward Ginza (2 stops on Ginza Line) for high-end sushi and tempura.
akasaka.lateNight: Akasaka itself quiets down at night, but Roppongi is a 15 min walk for late-night bars and clubs.

shibuya.title: Shibuya — Conference Area
shibuya.description: Trunk Hotel is on Cat Street in Jingumae, the stylish backstreet corridor between Shibuya and Harajuku. This is one of the best areas in Tokyo.
shibuya.gettingThere: From Akasaka-mitsuke: Ginza Line to Omotesando (10 min, 3 stops), walk 8 min to Trunk Hotel. OR Hanzomon Line from Nagatacho to Shibuya (direct, 10 min), walk 10 min.
nearTrunk: Cat Street — right outside, independent boutiques and cafes
Omotesando — 5 min walk, luxury brand flagships and stunning architecture
Meiji Shrine / Yoyogi Park — 15 min walk
shibuya.afterConference: Post-conference drinks: the streets between Cat Street and Shibuya are packed with izakayas and bars. Nonbei Yokocho (Drunkard's Alley) near the station is great for tiny atmospheric bars.

Comfortable walking shoes (you will walk 15,000-25,000 steps/day)
clothing: Layers — sweater, long sleeve, light base layer
Scarf and light gloves (mornings are cold)
One nicer outfit for fine dining (Den, Narisawa, etc.)
Slip-on shoes (easy to remove at temples, some restaurants)
tech: No power adapter needed (US plugs work in Japan)
Download Google Maps offline map for Tokyo
Download Google Translate Japanese offline pack
Set up Suica in Apple Wallet before you go
misc: Small day bag / packable tote (for shopping)
Ziplock bag for trash (public bins are rare)
Hand towel / handkerchief (many restrooms lack paper towels)
Cash: withdraw ¥20,000-30,000 on arrival at 7-Eleven ATM
Motion sickness meds if needed (some trains are crowded)
